pages.text: Philip II was the king of Macedon from 359 BC until his death in 336 BC. He changed Macedon from a small kingdom into a powerful nation that ruled Ancient Greece. He was also the father of Alexander the Great.

pages.text: Philip was born in either 383 or 382 BC. When he was young, he was held as a hostage in Thebes, which was then the leading city of Greece. While there, he received a military and diplomatic education from Epaminondas and lived with Pammenes.

pages.text: After his brother died in battle, Philip took control of Macedon. He worked very hard to improve his army. He created the Macedonian phalanx and gave his soldiers long spears called sarissas.
pages.caption: Great Tumulus of Aigai

evidence.articleCaption: Great Tumulus of Aigai

pages.text: With his strong new army, Philip defeated neighboring tribes and Greek city-states. After winning a big battle in 338 BC, he united the Greek states into a federation to plan an invasion.
pages.caption: Philip commissioned the construction of the Philippeion at Olympia to commemorate his victory at the Battle of Chaeronea

evidence.articleCaption: Philip commissioned the construction of the Philippeion at Olympia to commemorate his victory at the Battle of Chaeronea

pages.text: In October 336 BC, Philip went to a wedding celebration at Aigai. While walking into a theatre without bodyguards to look friendly, one of his own bodyguards stabbed and killed him.
After Philip died, his son Alexander became king immediately. Alexander went on to lead the planned invasion of the Persian Empire just as his father had wanted to do.

B1-B2.headline: The Rise and Fall of Philip II

pages.text: Philip II of Macedon ruled as king from 359 BC until his assassination in 336 BC. Through clever policies and military reforms, he transformed Macedon from a peripheral kingdom into the dominant power of Ancient Greece in less than twenty-five years. He was the father of Alexander the Great.

pages.text: Born as the youngest son of King Amyntas III, Philip experienced captivity in his youth. Held in Thebes, he received valuable military and diplomatic education before returning to Macedon and eventually seizing the throne after his brother died in battle.

pages.text: Philip radically reformed the Macedonian military. He vastly increased the cavalry, improved soldier discipline, and introduced the Macedonian phalanx armed with long sarissa spears. These innovations, combined with siege engines and diplomacy, enabled him to defeat rivals like the Illyrians and Paeonians.

pages.text: After defeating Athens and Thebes at the Battle of Chaeronea in 338 BC, Philip established the Hellenic League. As its elected hegemon and commander-in-chief, he prepared for a major invasion of the Achaemenid Empire.
pages.caption: Philip commissioned the construction of the Philippeion at Olympia to commemorate his victory at the Battle of Chaeronea

pages.text: In October 336 BC, Philip attended a marriage celebration at Aigai. While entering the town theatre unprotected to appear approachable to diplomats, he was stabbed by Pausanias of Orestis, one of his own bodyguards. The assassin was chased and killed during his escape attempt.

Philip's sudden death led to the immediate succession of his son Alexander. Ancient writers like Cleitarchus and Justin debated potential motives involving personal feuds or royal family intrigue, while modern historians view some of these accounts with skepticism, noting that Alexander immediately took his father's place.

Reigning from 359 BC until his assassination in 336 BC, Philip II of Macedon orchestrated the rapid ascent of his kingdom from a marginal regional state to the dominant geopolitical power of the Greek world. As a member of the Argead dynasty, he laid the administrative and military foundations that enabled his son, Alexander the Great, to subsequently launch an invasion of the Achaemenid Empire.

pages.text: Philip's formative years included a period as a political hostage in Thebes. There, he absorbed sophisticated military and diplomatic doctrines from prominent local statesmen. Upon returning to Macedon, he capitalized on a dynastic crisis following the death of his brother Perdiccas III in battle to bypass an infant heir and secure the throne.

pages.text: His military restructuring altered ancient warfare. Philip expanded the royal cavalry exponentially, instituted professional discipline with promotion pathways, and pioneered combined arms tactics alongside siege artillery. Crucially, he instituted the Macedonian phalanx, equipping infantrymen with the long sarissa polearm that became the tactical bedrock of his campaigns.
pages.caption: Great Tumulus of Aigai

evidence.articleCaption: Great Tumulus of Aigai

pages.text: Through strategic marriages, aggressive territorial expansion against Illyrians and Thracians, and diplomatic maneuvers during conflicts such as the Third Sacred War, Philip subdued key Greek rivals. The decisive victory at Chaeronea in 338 BC culminated in the establishment of the Hellenic League, positioning Philip as commander-in-chief for an impending pan-Hellenic expedition against Persia.
pages.caption: Philip commissioned the construction of the Philippeion at Olympia to commemorate his victory at the Battle of Chaeronea

evidence.articleCaption: Philip commissioned the construction of the Philippeion at Olympia to commemorate his victory at the Battle of Chaeronea

pages.text: Philip's ambitions were abruptly curtailed in October 336 BC at Aigai. While attending a dynastic wedding celebration and deliberately walking unprotected to cultivate rapport with foreign dignitaries, he was assassinated by Pausanias of Orestis, a royal bodyguard who was killed by pursuers during his attempted escape.

The assassination generated considerable historical speculation. Later accounts by writers like Cleitarchus and Justin alleged complex personal motives or royal complicity involving Olympias and Alexander. However, modern historical analysis often treats these dramatic narratives with caution, noting that while suspicion naturally fell on the primary beneficiaries, the alleged plots remain debated and difficult to substantiate conclusively.

title: The Evolution of Cultural Property Conservation
sourceTitle: Conservation and restoration of cultural property
attribution: Adapted from English Wikipedia contributors; see pinned revision and history. SAGA AI-assisted adaptation under CC BY-SA 4.0. Wikipedia does not endorse SAGA.

pages.text: The conservation and restoration of cultural property focuses on the protection and care of tangible cultural heritage. This field includes artworks, architecture, archaeology, and museum collections. Conservation activities involve preventive care, examination, documentation, research, treatment, and education for the future.
pages.caption: Conservation of the Horses of Saint Mark (Venice)

evidence.articleCaption: Conservation of the Horses of Saint Mark (Venice)

pages.text: In the past, artists were normally the people called upon to repair damaged artworks. Over time, science and art became closely connected. Scientists began to study how the environment damages works of art. Later, universities and museums started offering professional training and courses.
pages.caption: Revision and conservation of the Holy Trinity Column in Olomouc (Czech Republic) in 2006

evidence.articleCaption: Revision and conservation of the Holy Trinity Column in Olomouc (Czech Republic) in 2006

pages.text: Today, modern conservation laboratories use special equipment like microscopes and spectrometers. This equipment helps experts examine objects and understand their components. The collected data guides conservators in deciding the best treatments to provide for each unique object.
pages.caption: A temporary windowed partition along restoration work area in the cloister of the Church of St. Trophime, Arles

evidence.articleCaption: A temporary windowed partition along restoration work area in the cloister of the Church of St. Trophime, Arles

pages.text: Many cultural works are very sensitive to environmental conditions. Factors like temperature, humidity, and exposure to light can cause damage. Therefore, these valuable items must be protected in controlled environments where variables are maintained within safe limits.
pages.caption: Since 1998, Harvard University wraps some of the valuable statues on its campus, such as this "Chinese stele", with waterproof covers every winter, in order to protect them from erosion caused by acid rain.

evidence.fileTitle: File:Bixi stele (wrapped), Harvard University, Cambridge, MA - IMG 4607.JPG
evidence.articleCaption: Since 1998, Harvard University wraps some of the valuable statues on its campus, such as this "Chinese stele", with waterproof covers every winter, in order to protect them from erosion caused by acid rain.

pages.text: Modern conservation also focuses on sustainable practices. Professionals try to reduce waste, lower energy costs, and minimize the use of harmful solvents. These steps ensure that conservation work does not harm the environment or contribute to global warming.

pages.text: Historically, the care of cultural heritage was primarily aimed at fixing objects for continued use and aesthetic enjoyment, and artists were normally called upon to make repairs. During the 19th century, however, science and art became intertwined as researchers began studying how environmental factors damage works of art.

pages.text: As the field developed, museums began employing specialized chemists to establish scientific approaches to object care. In modern conservation laboratories, professionals routinely use advanced equipment such as microscopes, spectrometers, and x-ray instruments to examine cultural works and determine appropriate treatments.

Practitioners strive to reduce waste, lower energy costs, and minimize the use of toxic solvents, ensuring that their methods support both the preservation of artifacts and ecological responsibility.

C1-C2.headline: Principles and Practices in Cultural Heritage Conservation

pages.text: The conservation and restoration of cultural property encompasses the protection and stewardship of tangible cultural heritage, including diverse forms such as artworks, architecture, archaeology, and museum collections. This multidimensional field integrates preventive measures, rigorous examination, documentation, empirical research, treatment, and educational outreach.
pages.caption: Conservation of the Horses of Saint Mark (Venice)

evidence.articleCaption: Conservation of the Horses of Saint Mark (Venice)

pages.text: Historically dominated by artists who repaired damaged objects for continued utility and aesthetic appreciation, the discipline underwent a profound methodological shift during the 19th and early 20th centuries. The integration of scientific analysis into artifact care marked the transition from traditional craftsmanship to an empirical profession supported by specialized laboratory research.
pages.caption: Revision and conservation of the Holy Trinity Column in Olomouc (Czech Republic) in 2006

evidence.articleCaption: Revision and conservation of the Holy Trinity Column in Olomouc (Czech Republic) in 2006

pages.text: Contemporary conservation laboratories employ sophisticated diagnostic instrumentation, including microscopes, spectrometers, and x-ray equipment. The empirical data derived from these analyses informs conservators as they evaluate physical needs, material properties, and ethical considerations to determine optimal treatment strategies.
pages.caption: A temporary windowed partition along restoration work area in the cloister of the Church of St. Trophime, Arles

evidence.articleCaption: A temporary windowed partition along restoration work area in the cloister of the Church of St. Trophime, Arles

pages.text: Preventive conservation is critical because numerous cultural artifacts exhibit high vulnerability to ambient environmental fluctuations. Maintaining strict parameters for temperature, relative humidity, visible light, and ultraviolet radiation within controlled storage and display environments is essential for mitigating cumulative material degradation.
pages.caption: Since 1998, Harvard University wraps some of the valuable statues on its campus, such as this "Chinese stele", with waterproof covers every winter, in order to protect them from erosion caused by acid rain.

pages.text: More recently, the profession has emphasized sustainable conservation practices to align institutional workflows with environmental responsibility. By actively reducing waste, lowering energy consumption, and restricting the deployment of harmful solvents, cultural institutions seek to minimize their ecological footprint while continuing their stewardship duties.

title: Cartography and Exploration in Iberia
attribution: Adapted from English Wikipedia contributors; see pinned revision and history. SAGA AI-assisted adaptation under CC BY-SA 4.0. Wikipedia does not endorse SAGA.

pages.text: Maps played a big part in the expansion of kingdoms in the Iberian Peninsula during the fourteenth to sixteenth centuries. They helped sailors, explorers, and navigators find their way across the seas. The Crown of Aragon controlled important trade routes in the Mediterranean Sea.
pages.caption: Dating from 1375, the full 8 sheet Catalan Atlas made by Abraham Cresques, cartographer to King Pere IV of Aragon. It was a gift from the King of the Crown of Aragon to the King of France. Many later maps and "portolan charts" are copies of this original Catalan one.

evidence.articleCaption: Dating from 1375, the full 8 sheet Catalan Atlas made by Abraham Cresques, cartographer to King Pere IV of Aragon. It was a gift from the King of the Crown of Aragon to the King of France. Many later maps and "portolan charts" are copies of this original Catalan one.

pages.text: Maps made travel easier by saving resources and time. Cartographers added wind patterns, latitude, and longitude to sea charts. Surveyors also used maps to plan out landmasses in places that were not yet fully explored, such as the Americas.
pages.caption: A pre-Mercator nautical chart of 1571, from Portuguese cartographer Fernão Vaz Dourado (c. 1520–c. 1580). It belongs to the so-called plane chart model, where observed latitudes and magnetic directions are plotted directly into the plane, with a constant scale, as if the Earth were plane (Portuguese National Archives of Torre do Tombo, Lisbon).

pages.text: Before maps were common for travel, people used them as decorative gifts for kings and popes. The Catalan Atlas from 1375 is a famous example of a decorated map. It was given as a gift to the King of France.
pages.caption: Portolan chart by Jorge de Aguiar (1492), the oldest known signed and dated chart of Portuguese origin (Beinecke Rare Book and Manuscript Library, University of Yale, New Haven, USA)

pages.text: Map makers used different styles over time. Early maps included drawings of paradise, angels, and mythical creatures. Later, maps began to show real regions and provinces with more accurate details as trade and geographical knowledge grew.
pages.caption: Americae Sive Qvartae Orbis Partis Nova Et Exactissima Descriptio, 1562

pages.text: Portolan charts appeared before the fourteenth century and were oriented to the north. They used compass bearings and scaled distances. These charts helped sailors travel farther onto open water without getting lost.

During the fourteenth to sixteenth centuries, cartography played a vital role in the expansion of Iberian kingdoms. These maps served primarily as navigational tools for sailors and explorers. The Crown of Aragon controlled significant trade routes across the Mediterranean Sea as part of the Silk Road.

pages.text: Darb El Arba'in is a very old trade road in Africa. People called it the Forty Days Road because the trip was said to take forty days long ago. It is the easternmost of the great north and south Trans-Saharan trade routes used to move many items.
pages.caption: Sudanese telegraph stamp depicting camel caravan (1898)

evidence.articleCaption: Sudanese telegraph stamp depicting camel caravan (1898)

pages.text: The journey from North Darfur, Sudan, to Asyut, Egypt, is approximately 1,800 km and usually took closer to 60 days. This time was needed to rest and water the herd along the desert route. Traveling this way was more direct, less expensive, and safer than taking the Nile route.
pages.caption: Map of Bir Natrun, a stop on the trade route that was known as a valuable source of rock salt (1925)

imageProvenance.credit: Drawn by O.M. Atabaney Sudan. Maṣlaḥat al-Misāḥah, cartographer.

evidence.articleCaption: Map of Bir Natrun, a stop on the trade route that was known as a valuable source of rock salt (1925)

pages.text: The desert here gets very little rain each year. It is very likely the driest region on earth. The road is set up so that water is always found within a few days of travel, and no single waterless stage is too long.
pages.caption: Viceroy of Kush Amenhotep called Huy receiving tribute from a Nubian embassy. c. 1332 – 1323 BC, TT40, Qurnet Murai, Luxor, Egypt

pages.text: Traders moved many goods on this path, including gold, salt, ivory, and spices. Caravans also moved slaves across the desert. The slave trade was stopped and blocked in the last decade of the nineteenth century.

pages.text: The route is still active today. People now use cars and trucks on asphalt roads along with camels and donkeys. Archeologists studying the route have found old watering stations, wayfinding markers, and camel bones.

B1-B2.headline: Journey on the Forty Days Road

pages.text: Darb El Arba'in, also known as the Forty Days Road, is the easternmost of the great north-south Trans-Saharan trade routes. Historically, travelers used this path to move trade goods, livestock, and slaves through a chain of oases from the African interior to the Nile River.

pages.text: The journey spans approximately 1,800 kilometers from North Darfur in Sudan to the Asyut Governorate in Egypt. Although traditionally said to take forty days, the trip usually required closer to sixty days because travelers needed to rest and water their herds.

C1-C2.headline: Trade and Travel on Darb El Arba'in

pages.text: Darb El Arba'in functions as the easternmost of the major north-south Trans-Saharan trade routes. Historically designated as the Forty Days Road based on traditional travel duration estimates, the route facilitated the movement of commodities, livestock, and human captives from the interior of Africa toward portage points on the Nile River.
pages.caption: Sudanese telegraph stamp depicting camel caravan (1898)

evidence.articleCaption: Sudanese telegraph stamp depicting camel caravan (1898)

pages.text: Spanning approximately 1,800 kilometers between North Darfur in Sudan and the Asyut Governorate in Egypt, the transit typically necessitated roughly sixty days rather than forty to accommodate herd maintenance and watering requirements. Traveling through the desert offered a more direct and cost-effective alternative to Nile-adjacent pathways.
pages.caption: Map of Bir Natrun, a stop on the trade route that was known as a valuable source of rock salt (1925)

imageProvenance.credit: Drawn by O.M. Atabaney Sudan. Maṣlaḥat al-Misāḥah, cartographer.

pages.text: Traversing what is very likely the driest region on earth, the route depends on strategic spacing where water is accessible within a three-day window, ensuring no single waterless segment exceeds 280 kilometers. This design sustained main north-south commercial traffic across an extremely arid landscape.

pages.text: Commercial exchanges along the corridor encompassed an extensive array of goods, ranging from gold and ivory to spices and textiles. Concurrently, the route sustained a severe slave trade originating from regions beyond Nubia until the Anglo-Egyptian government abolished and blockaded the practice during the final decade of the nineteenth century.

pages.text: Contemporary archaeological investigations along the corridor have identified structural remains, wayfinding cairns, and petroglyphs spanning periods from the New Kingdom to the Roman era. The route persists today, accommodating modern vehicular traffic alongside traditional camel drives across sand and rock.
